Mysterious 1,000-Mile Cloud on Mars May Reveal Hitherto Unseen Atmospheric Physics

A Recurring Martian Mystery

Every morning during the Martian spring and summer, a thin, extraordinarily long cloud forms near the towering volcano Arsia Mons. Over the course of the morning, the formation stretches over 1,000 miles—roughly the distance from New York City to Kansas City—before completely dissipating. The cycle then repeats day after day for several months.

First recorded by a space probe in 2018, this recurring atmospheric phenomenon is known as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). Until recently, planetary scientists lacked a plausible explanation for how such a massive structure could form and vanish with such regularity.

Simulating Exotic Physics

Researchers have now successfully modeled the cloud's formation for the first time. Published in Nature Geoscience, the new study indicates that the AMEC may be driven by a physical process that has never been directly observed in the atmosphere of any planet.

"We found that we needed to include some exotic physics… physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before," said Jorge Hernández-Bernal, a planetary scientist at Sorbonne Université in Paris and lead author of the study. "Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped."

Homogeneous Nucleation Under Extreme Conditions

On Earth, clouds typically form when water vapor condenses into droplets or ice crystals around tiny microscopic particles like dust or salt. However, the new study suggests that the Martian cloud forms through a process called homogeneous nucleation. In this scenario, vapor changes directly into ice crystals entirely on its own, without any seeding debris.

"It’s akin to droplets of condensation appearing in the middle of a room, rather than on a window," Hernández-Bernal explained.

Achieving homogeneous nucleation requires extreme meteorological conditions: a sharp temperature drop of 30° Celsius within just 10 minutes, paired with exceptionally high relative humidity. The 65,000-foot-tall Arsia Mons volcano acts as a catalyst; when regional wind currents strike the massive volcanic structure, they generate a powerful wave that launches moist air high into the atmosphere within minutes.

Broader Implications and Reader Verification

While scientists have theorized that homogeneous nucleation could occur in the upper atmospheres of other terrestrial planets, including Venus and Earth, it has never been documented in nature. Earth's atmosphere lacks the necessary extreme conditions, requiring humidity levels more than 100,000 times greater than any value ever recorded on our planet.

What is Confirmed vs. Unknown

  • Confirmed: Researchers successfully replicated the AMEC in computer simulations by incorporating theoretical homogeneous nucleation physics, supported by data regarding Mars' local topography and temperature drops.
  • Unknown: Direct observational confirmation of the physical process in action remains limited, and the full extent of high-altitude humidity variations across Mars requires further study.

Readers can review the peer-reviewed findings directly in the journal Nature Geoscience or read the original reporting via the [Ars Technica coverage](https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/a-1000-mile-cloud-on-mars-may-reveal-physics-never-seen-in-nature/).
